generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, succeeding depends as much on how you manage your own learning as on raw ability. Self-regulated learning means directing your own study: setting a clear goal, monitoring whether your approach is actually working against your results, and changing it when it is not. Self-efficacy, the belief that you can master something difficult, is what keeps you working at a hard topic long enough to crack it. That belief is built mostly from small wins, each one proof that effort pays.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who hit the same wall: a topic in their course that they find genuinely hard.

{{learner-a}} keeps doing what has always worked before, re-reading the chapter and the lecture notes, and gets the same blank result each time. When a low mark comes back, {{learner-a}} decides the problem is simply a lack of talent for the subject and quietly eases off. The effort was real, but nothing was monitored and nothing was changed, and the belief that the topic could be cracked drained away.

{{learner-b}} hits the same wall but treats it as information. Noticing that re-reading is not working, {{learner-b}} switches to practising the hard parts directly and testing whether each attempt goes better than the last. It does, a little, and that small win rebuilds the confidence to keep going. This is self-regulated learning with self-efficacy intact.

Both students worked hard. Only {{learner-b}} regulated the learning, monitoring what was happening and adjusting, and protected the belief that persistence would pay.
generatedProse.summary: Succeeding rests on an engine: self-regulated learning, the habit of steering your own study by setting goals, checking your progress against your results, and adjusting what you do. Self-efficacy is the belief that keeps that engine running when a topic is hard, and it grows mostly through small experiences of mastery. You can now explain how this engine works, weigh the part self-efficacy plays in sustaining effort, and judge whether a student in an example is genuinely regulating their learning.

check.body: In the worked example, what best explains why {{learner-b}} kept going when {{learner-a}} gave up?

items.text: A small win rebuilt {{learner-b}}'s self-efficacy, the belief that persistence would pay off.
{{learner-b}} was naturally more talented at the subject than {{learner-a}}.
{{learner-b}} had an easier version of the task to complete.
{{learner-b}} simply spent far more hours on it than {{learner-a}} did.

feedback.correct: That's right. A small experience of mastery rebuilt {{learner-b}}'s self-efficacy, and that belief sustained the effort.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what changed {{learner-b}}'s belief that the hard topic could be cracked.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} kept going because a small win rebuilt self-efficacy. Natural talent, an easier task and extra hours are not what the example turns on.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
